ui.eyebrow: CATHORA / Jewelry from the sacred lands
ui.lede: Before you ever heard its name, it was already on its way to you. Pieces shaped by sacred mountains, old wisdom, and the wish you carry.
ui.landsH:
Five places where people
have gone to make a wish.
ui.landsP: For a thousand years, people have climbed these stone steps asking for the oldest things: safety on the road, a child in good health, a year of good fortune. Each chapter carries the legend of one place.
ui.elP: Water feeds wood, wood feeds fire, fire returns to earth, earth gives birth to metal, metal calls back the water. The old sages believed every life turns within this wheel — and that what you keep close can lean it, gently, toward the light.
ui.storyH:
One for every worry
the heart can hold.
ui.story1: Dawn, in the mountains of eastern China. Mist rises from the valley like the breath of a sleeping animal. Somewhere above the pines, a bell — once, then again, one hundred and eight times. By the last note, the mountain has taken them all.
ui.story2: Cathay was the West's old name for China. Ora is Latin, to pray.
ui.newsP: New moons, solar terms and the turning of the year — a quiet note when the season changes, and first word of each new chapter.

putuo.subtitle: Island of Compassion
putuo.legend: Where the tide is said to chant, and sailors once prayed for home.
putuo.known: The sea, the tide caves, Guanyin
putuo.lead: An island at the edge of the East China Sea, where the land runs out and the prayers begin.
putuo.close: This chapter is for safe passage, and for the ones you wait for.
putuo.s1: More than a thousand years ago, a monk from Japan set sail for home with a statue of Guanyin, the bodhisattva who hears the cries of the world. Near this island the sea rose and would not let him pass. Each time he tried, the waves turned him back. So he left her here — and she is called, still, the Guanyin Who Would Not Leave.
putuo.s2: In the caves along the shore, the tide breaks with a sound like chanting. Fishermen once listened to it before they put out to sea. Their wives climbed the hills before dawn, watched the horizon, and asked for only one thing: that the boats come home.
putuo.s3: At first light the sun rises straight out of the water, and for a moment the whole sea turns the colour of sunstone.

lingyin.subtitle: Hidden Spirit
lingyin.legend: A peak that flew from a distant land, and chose to stay.
lingyin.known: The Peak That Flew Here, stone Buddhas, old trees
lingyin.lead: In the hills west of the lake, a peak stands where it does not belong.
lingyin.close: This chapter is for clarity, and for the quiet voice that already knows.
lingyin.s1: Some seventeen centuries ago, a monk named Huili came here from India. He looked up at the peak and was astonished, for it was a mountain from his homeland. "When did it fly here?" he asked. It has been called the Peak That Flew Here ever since. At its foot he founded a temple and named it Lingyin — the place where the spirit hides.
lingyin.s2: The spirit is hiding still. Carved into the rock, stone Buddhas smile in the half-dark. Incense drifts through the old trees. People come here to ask for wisdom, for an answer, for a sign that they are on the right road.

jingshan.subtitle: Mountain of Tea and Zen
jingshan.legend: A single bowl of tea crossed the sea and became a way of life.
jingshan.lead: On a mountain north-west of Hangzhou, the path climbs through bamboo so dense that the light turns green.
jingshan.close: This chapter is for calm, and for doing one thing with your whole heart.
jingshan.s1: For centuries this was one of the great Zen temples of the south. Monks grew tea on the slopes and served it to guests in a slow, silent ceremony: water heated, tea whisked, a bowl passed from hand to hand.
jingshan.s2: Monks from Japan crossed the sea to study here. When they went home they carried the bowls, the seeds and the silence with them. In time it became the Way of Tea.
jingshan.s3: Everything that matters can fit in one bowl. That is what the mountain teaches.

tiantai.subtitle: Terrace of Heaven
tiantai.legend: A mountain named for the stars it was said to stand beneath.
tiantai.known: Layered peaks, an ancient temple, the poet Cold Mountain
tiantai.lead: A mountain of folded peaks, named by the ancients for the Terrace stars it was said to stand beneath.
tiantai.close: This chapter is for new beginnings, and for the path you have not taken yet.
tiantai.s1: At its foot stands a temple founded more than fourteen centuries ago, beside a stream that has never stopped running. A school of Buddhism was born here, and travelled to Japan and Korea, where it is still alive today.
tiantai.s2: Long ago, two laughing strangers were often seen at the temple kitchen door. One of them was the poet Hanshan — Cold Mountain — who wrote his poems on rocks, on trees and on walls, then walked into the mountain without leaving a name.
tiantai.s3: Some journeys begin by going up.

emei.subtitle: Mountain of Golden Light
emei.legend: Above a sea of clouds, pilgrims still wait for a halo of light.
emei.known: The Golden Summit, the sea of clouds, the Buddha's light
emei.lead: In the west of China, a mountain rises through the clouds to a summit of gold.
emei.close: This chapter is for good fortune, and for the light that finds you when you have climbed far enough.
emei.s1: Pilgrims climb for days to reach it. At the top they stand at the edge of a sea of cloud, and wait. Sometimes, when the sun is behind them, a ring of rainbow light appears on the clouds below — and inside it, their own shadow, haloed. The people of the mountain call it the Buddha's light. They say it does not come to everyone.
emei.s2: Thirteen centuries ago, the poet Li Bai watched a half-moon of autumn hang over this mountain and wrote it into a poem that is still taught in China's schools.

longmen.subtitle: A Thousand Years in Stone
longmen.legend: On the cliffs above the Yi River, a hundred thousand Buddhas have sat in silence for fifteen centuries.
longmen.known: The Vairocana Buddha, the Yi River, cave carvings
longmen.lead: South of Luoyang, the Yi River runs between two hills that face each other like the towers of a gate. The ancients called it the Dragon Gate.
longmen.s1: From the Northern Wei to the Tang, for more than four hundred years, craftsmen cut into the limestone, stroke by stroke, until more than a hundred thousand figures filled the cliffs — the smallest two centimetres high, the largest seventeen metres.
longmen.s2: The great Vairocana Buddha of Fengxian is said to have been carved in the likeness of an empress. Eyes lowered, half smiling, she watches the river — and everyone who looks up at her.
longmen.s3: Fifteen hundred years of wind and rain, and the stone remembers every cut. Some things are meant to be made slowly, one mark at a time.
longmen.close: This chapter is for endurance, and for the things that take time to become.

whitehorse.subtitle: The First Temple
whitehorse.legend: A white horse carried the scriptures across thousands of miles, and the teaching arrived in China.
whitehorse.known: China's first temple, the Qiyun Pagoda, the white horse
whitehorse.lead: In the year 68, outside the walls of Luoyang, China built its first Buddhist temple.
whitehorse.s1: The story goes that Emperor Ming dreamed one night of a golden figure, glowing, flying in from the west. He sent envoys to find it, and far away they met two monks and asked them to come east.
whitehorse.s2: A white horse carried the scriptures and images all the way back to Luoyang beside them. To remember it, the new temple was named for the horse.
whitehorse.s3: A dream, a long road, two strangers and a horse. Perhaps every meeting that matters begins like this.
whitehorse.close: This chapter is for journeys, and for the people who travelled far to find you.

wudang.subtitle: Mountain of Taiji
wudang.legend: A Taoist mountain in the clouds, where Tai Chi drew its first circle.
wudang.known: The Golden Hall, the Purple Cloud Palace, Tai Chi
wudang.lead: In the mountains of Hubei, seventy-two peaks all seem to bow toward one point: the gilded bronze hall on the summit of Heaven's Pillar.
wudang.s1: Taoists believe the world turns between yin and yang — stillness and motion, again and again. Legend says a hermit here once watched a magpie fight a snake, softness against strength, and in that moment understood Tai Chi.
wudang.s2: Six hundred years ago an emperor ordered palaces built across the mountain, and the summit hall was cast in bronze and covered in gold. In summer storms lightning strikes its roof in a sea of fire — and the hall stands untouched.
wudang.s3: The soft overcomes the hard; stillness masters motion. Real strength is often just staying steady.
wudang.close: This chapter is for balance, and for standing steady in the storm.

wood.name: Wood
wood.desc: Wood is the green force of spring — the shoot that splits the stone. It rises, it reaches, it begins again. Those born under Wood are said to carry the courage to start.

fire.name: Fire
fire.desc: Fire is summer at noon, a lamp in a dark room. It warms, it gathers people, it lights the way. Fire is said to bring brightness, passion, and the luck that follows those who shine.

earth.name: Earth
earth.desc: Earth is the ground beneath every season — patient, generous, holding everything up. Earth is said to bring stability, trust, and a harvest that comes in its own time.

metal.name: Metal
metal.desc: Metal is autumn air, a bell's clear note, the edge of a blade. It cuts away what is not needed. Metal is said to bring clarity, resolve, and a clean kind of protection.

water.name: Water
water.desc: Water is winter and the deep sea. It is soft, yet it wears through stone; it takes the shape of everything, and keeps its own. Water is said to bring wisdom, intuition, and the patience to flow.

brand.name1: Cathay was the old Western name for China — the word Marco Polo used. Silk, tea, and mountains wrapped in mist.
brand.name2: Ora is Latin for "pray." Where the two meet is Cathora — a prayer from Cathay.
brand.p1: Before you ever heard its name, it was already on its way to you. The Chinese call this yuan — the thread of fate that ties a person to a place, a moment, a wish.
brand.p2: Dawn, in the mountains of eastern China. Mist rises from the valley like the breath of a sleeping animal. Somewhere above the pines, a bell — once, then again, one hundred and eight times. One for every worry the heart can hold. By the last note, the mountain has taken them all.
brand.p3: For more than a thousand years, people have come to China's old temples to ask for the oldest things: safety, good health, a year of good fortune. They believed that luck, like water, finds those who make room for it.
brand.p4: We carry that belief to you. Wood that has gathered its fragrance for decades. Seeds named for the tree where the Buddha awoke. Stones the mountain kept in its dark heart for ten thousand years — each long believed to hold a blessing, a protection, a quiet turning toward the good.
brand.p5: A circle has no beginning and no end. Neither does good fortune. It never stays; it only moves — from hand to hand, from one wish to the next. Wear it, and let it move toward you.
brand.p6: We cannot promise you luck. But we know where it has always been waited for: in stillness, in intention, in a small circle of beads resting against the pulse of your wrist.
brand.pc: Cathora carries that wish to you. Every piece comes from a sacred land and holds a single blessing, and part of every purchase returns to the temples that keep the tradition alive.
brand.qiH: The Five Elements: the breathing of heaven and earth.
brand.q1: Everything breathes. The mountain breathes in mist. The river breathes in light. A stone asleep for ten thousand years breathes so slowly that only the patient can hear it. The ancient Chinese called this breath qi, and believed it moves through all things — through the earth, through the stars, through you.
brand.q2: Water nourishing wood, wood feeding fire, fire returning to earth, earth giving birth to metal, metal calling back the water — five elements in an endless wheel, and every life turning within it. When the wheel turns your way, they called it good fortune.
brand.q3: So we choose each material by its element and by the energy it has long been said to carry. The Book of Changes says nothing stays still: fortune rises, falls, and rises again. A bracelet cannot hold back the tide. But each time it warms against your skin, it can remind you to turn with it — toward the light.
brand.pr1: Cultural history, collaboration records and creative interpretation are different things. We explain each clearly.
brand.pr2: Form, finish, proportion and fit give meaning a physical presence. The piece has to work as jewelry first.
brand.pr3: A piece can mark a change, carry a thought, or simply become something you love to wear.
brand.founderH: A brand has a perspective. There is a person behind it.
brand.founderP: Why these places, and why jewelry.
brand.creditsP: Photographs of the sacred lands come from Wikimedia Commons and are used under their respective licenses, cropped for display. No institutional endorsement is implied.
brand.n1: Cathay is the old Western name for China. Silk, tea, and mountains in the mist.
brand.n3: Cathora — a prayer from Cathay, following an invisible thread all the way to your wrist.
brand.s1: Before you ever heard its name, it was already on its way to you. The Chinese call this yuan — an invisible thread that ties a person to a place, a moment, a wish.
brand.s2: In China's sacred mountains and old temples, people have made wishes for more than a thousand years. A safe journey. A healthy child. A smooth year. They tied red threads to the branches, turned beads between their fingers, and walked back down believing that luck, like water, flows toward those who make room for it.
brand.s3: The Book of Changes says: one yin, one yang — that is the Way. All things move between fullness and emptiness, and fortune is no different: it never stays, it only passes through. A wish cannot hold on to luck. But in the moment of wishing, a person grows still — and so, when luck passes by, they recognise it.
brand.s4: CATHORA begins in these places. Each collection belongs to a sacred land; each piece tells you its origin, its element and its meaning. Natural wood, stone and silver, in simple forms made to be worn every day.
brand.s5: We do not promise luck. We only want an old wish to have a quiet place in your life. Keep a wish close.
brand.qiQuote: "Heaven has five phases — water, fire, metal, wood, earth. Each in its season nurtures and transforms, and so all things are made." — Kongzi Jiayu
brand.qi1: The Five Elements are not five substances but five xing — five ways of moving. Three thousand years ago, the Book of Documents put it like this: water soaks downward; fire flares upward; wood bends and straightens; metal yields and is reshaped; earth receives the seed and gives the harvest. The ancients were not looking at things themselves, but at how things change.
brand.qi2: Between the five, there is giving rise and there is holding back. Wood feeds fire, fire makes earth, earth bears metal, metal carries water, water nourishes wood. And wood parts earth, earth dams water, water quenches fire, fire melts metal, metal cuts wood. Giving rise is generosity; holding back is restraint. With only generosity, things would grow wild and lose their order; with only restraint, they would wither. Heaven and earth endure because every force is both supported and contained. This is what the Chinese call he, harmony — not the absence of conflict, but a sense of measure within it.
brand.lede: Bringing the wishes of China's sacred mountains into everyday life.
brand.s4b: A circle has no beginning and no end. A ring of beads is a small universe of its own: always returning, never ceasing.
brand.qi3: The ancients believed heaven and humankind are one: the body is a small heaven and earth. Liver is wood, heart is fire, spleen is earth, lungs are metal, kidneys are water; the seasons and the directions each belong to an element too. As the breath of the world turns, a person's breath rises and falls with it. What we call fortune is only the relationship between you and the rhythm of the world — move with the season and things flow; move against it and they stall. The Yellow Emperor's Classic advises: in spring and summer, nourish yang; in autumn and winter, nourish yin. To move in step is itself a practice.
brand.qi4: The year, month, day and hour of a person's birth each correspond to a pair of heavenly stems and earthly branches — eight characters in all, the bazi. Among those eight, some elements are abundant and some are scarce. The ancients did not call this fate. They called it endowment: the particular breath you were born carrying. What is too strong may be eased; what is weak may be supported. Balance is not about changing your destiny. It is about knowing it — where you come from, what you lack, and where you are going.
brand.qi5: Today we describe something similar in a different language. Physics tells us that, at bottom, everything is energy and vibration. Biology has found that our sleep, body temperature and moods rise and fall with day and night and with the seasons — that we carry an invisible clock inside us. Psychology tells us that when a person knows clearly what they want, they are quicker to notice opportunity, and to take it. The ancients had none of these words. But with qi and the Five Elements they were saying the same thing: a person and the world move to one rhythm.
brand.el_water_p: Water benefits all things and does not contend. It teaches softness, and persistence — the softest thing can wear through the hardest.
brand.el_wood_p: Wood grows upward and roots downward. However high the branches reach, the roots must go as deep.
brand.el_fire_p: Fire gives light and warmth. It teaches passion, and this: when one lamp lights another, it loses none of its own light.
brand.el_earth_p: Earth carries everything and says nothing. Seasons turn; it is always there. Great virtue bears all things.
brand.el_metal_p: Metal becomes a vessel only through a thousand blows of the hammer. It teaches resolve, and letting go — autumn drops its leaves for the sake of spring.
brand.qi6: So the Five Elements were never about fate. They are about balance. When your elements are in harmony, your qi flows; when your qi flows, your heart settles; when your heart is settled, you see clearly, and opportunity and the right people find it easier to reach you. That, more or less, is what the ancients meant by good fortune. Draw close to what you lack: keep green things near to nourish wood, spend time by water to replenish water, and wear natural stone, wood and silver, so that the element you need stays with you, close to the skin, every day.
brand.qi7: What did your elements look like at the moment you were born? Which one runs strong, and which runs short? Find out first. Knowing yourself is where all good fortune begins.

founder.h1:
A brand has a perspective.
There is a person behind it.
founder.p1: This space is for the founder's own words: the first time in those mountains, why jewelry, and what the founder hopes the wearer will carry.
founder.note: Portrait and biography await the founder's contribution. No personal history has been invented here.
founder.f1: As a child, I followed my grandmother each spring to a temple in the mountains, up the stone steps one at a time. The mountain was quiet. All I could hear was the bell, and my own breathing.
founder.f2: On the way down, she tied a red thread around my wrist. Wear this, she said. It keeps you safe. I asked how a piece of string could keep anyone safe. She smiled. "The string can't. The heart can."
founder.f3: It took me many years to understand. I left home to study and to work, and moved many times. The red thread never shielded me from anything. But in every uncertain moment, it reminded me that someone had once held me in their thoughts like that.
founder.f4: The winter my grandmother died, I went back to that mountain alone. The stone steps were the same steps; there was just no one beside me. I stood in front of the main hall for a long time, not knowing what to ask for. An old monk sweeping the courtyard came over and asked, "What have you come to ask for?" I said I didn't know. He nodded. "Not knowing is fine too."
founder.f5: He pointed to the mountain behind him. "Most people come here to ask for something — safety, money, love. Look at this mountain. It asks for nothing, so it has everything. When the clouds come, it holds them; when they go, it doesn't hold on."
founder.f6: On the way down I remembered a line from the Tao Te Ching: "In learning, one gains a little every day; in the Way, one lets go a little every day." Seeking knowledge is adding; seeking the Way is subtracting. Maybe making a wish was never about getting more. Maybe in the moment you say it, you set down everything extra — until only the one thing you truly care about remains.
founder.fq: "The mountain asks for nothing, so it has everything."
founder.f7: The Buddhists say the world we see is born of the mind. Zhuangzi spoke of the fasting of the heart: emptiness is the fasting of the heart. Only when the heart is empty can good things come in. Whatever protects us, it is always the heart that is being protected: when the heart is settled, the road becomes clear; when the heart is at peace, fortune follows.
founder.f8: The Chinese say that objects carry the Way. There is nothing mysterious about a thread or a string of beads. What is mysterious is the intention a person places in it — and the quiet steadiness that intention grows into, day after day, as it is worn. An old saying goes: a person nourishes the jade, and the jade nourishes the person. As you wear it, it keeps you company, and slowly becomes part of you.
founder.f9: That is the kind of object CATHORA wants to make: one with an origin you can name, a form that rewards a close look, and room for meaning of your own. It doesn't ask for anything on your behalf. It only touches your wrist lightly when the day gets loud, and reminds you: come back.
founder.f10: I cannot make a wish for you. But I hope that when you put it on, you think of someone who once prayed for you — or become the one who prays for someone else. A circle has no beginning and no end. Neither does a blessing.

wealth.desc: Not sudden riches — abundance that flows like water, steady and long, that arrives and stays.

love.name: Love
love.line: For the thread that ties two people.
love.desc: The Chinese believe in yuan — an invisible red thread already tied between two people. For those still waiting, and those holding on.

q1.a: We don't make that claim. Each design draws on the prayer traditions of Chinese mountain temples, we work alongside temple communities, and part of every purchase returns to them. When a piece is part of a real ceremony, we will say exactly where and when.

q2.a: Yes. Only natural woods, seeds and stones, and 925 silver — never dyed glass or plastic. The exact material of each piece is listed under Specifications.

q3.a: We use a high-tension elastic cord that lasts with normal wear. Roll it on over your palm rather than stretching it. If it ever breaks, contact us and we'll help.

q4.q: Can I send it as a gift?
